relearning.title: Read: naming compounds from formulas
relearning.description: A short reading with the drink-size analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can take the chemical formula of a compound and write its name, ionic or covalent, including polyatomic ions and transition metals.**

**Think of ordering a drink.** If a shop sells lemonade in only one size, you just say "a lemonade." If it sells coffee in small and large, you have to say which size. Metals work the same way. Calcium only comes in one "size" (Ca²⁺), so you just say **calcium**. Iron comes in two (Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺), so you must say which one: **iron(II)** or **iron(III)**.

**Step 1 is always: ionic or covalent?** Metal + nonmetal (or any polyatomic ion, like ammonium) = **ionic**. Two nonmetals = **covalent**. The two systems have different rules, so decide first.

**Ionic names:** metal first, then the nonmetal with an **-ide** ending (chlorine → chloride, oxygen → oxide, nitrogen → nitride, phosphorus → phosphide). **No prefixes, ever.** A **polyatomic ion keeps its own name** with no -ide (sodium nitrate, ammonium chloride).

**Covalent names:** use prefixes (mono 1, di 2, tri 3, tetra 4, penta 5, hexa 6). The first element gets a prefix **except mono**. The second element always gets a prefix and an -ide ending.

**Worked example:** Mg₃P₂. Mg is a metal and P is a nonmetal, so it is ionic. Magnesium is in Group 2, so no Roman numeral. Phosphorus → phosphide. No prefixes, even with 3 Mg and 2 P. Answer: **magnesium phosphide**.

checks.prompt: What is the correct name of BaCl₂?
checks.explanation: Barium is a metal, so BaCl₂ is ionic: no prefixes. Barium is in Group 2 and is always +2, so it gets no Roman numeral. Adding di- for the 2 chlorines is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Nitrogen and fluorine are both nonmetals. Complete the name of NF₃: nitrogen ___
checks.explanation: Covalent, so use prefixes: tri- for 3 fluorines, and fluorine becomes fluoride. Nitrogen gets no mono. Leaving out the prefix (nitrogen fluoride) is the common mistake.

sections.title: Roman numerals and harder names

body.text:
**Which metals get a Roman numeral?** Group 1, 2 and 13 metals have only one charge, so they **never** get one. Metals that can have more than one charge (Fe, Cu, Pb, Sn and other transition metals) **always** get one. The numeral is the size of the charge, not the number of atoms.

**Finding the Roman numeral (reverse criss-cross):** find the total negative charge from the anions, make the metals cancel it, then divide by the number of metal atoms. ALWAYS double check that the charges add to zero. If a formula like FeO has no subscripts, it may have been reduced, so do the math instead of guessing.

**Worked example 2:** Fe₂(CO₃)₃ (carbonate is CO₃²⁻). Iron needs a numeral. Total negative: 3 × (−2) = −6. Two irons must total +6, so each iron is +6 ÷ 2 = +3. Check: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. Carbonate keeps its name. Answer: **iron(III) carbonate**.

**Worked example 3:** N₂O₅. Both are nonmetals, so it is covalent: use prefixes. 2 nitrogens → dinitrogen; 5 oxygens → pentoxide. Answer: **dinitrogen pentoxide**.

**Watch out for:** prefixes on ionic compounds ("calcium dichloride"), numerals on Group 1, 2 or 13 metals ("magnesium(II) oxide"), using the metal's subscript as its numeral (Fe₂O₃ is not iron(II)), putting -ide on a polyatomic ion ("sodium sulfide" for Na₂SO₄), leaving out covalent prefixes ("phosphorus chloride") and putting mono on the first element.

checks.prompt: Chloride is Cl⁻. What is the correct name of CuCl₂?
checks.explanation: Two Cl⁻ give −2, so the one copper is +2: copper(II) chloride. Check: +2 + 2(−1) = 0. Choosing copper(I) because there is 1 copper atom is the common mistake, and ionic names never use prefixes like di-.

checks.prompt: Sulfate is SO₄²⁻. What is the charge on the lead ion in Pb(SO₄)₂? Type the number only (for +3, type 3).
checks.explanation: Two SO₄²⁻ give 2(−2) = −4, so the one lead is +4: lead(IV) sulfate. Check: +4 + 2(−2) = 0. Using the 2 outside the parentheses as lead's charge is the common mistake.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain why BaO is named barium oxide and not barium(II) oxide or barium monoxide.

relearning.title: Do: flip the naming rules, then name one step by step
relearning.description: Flashcards with a 3-question self-quiz, then a name worked out one step at a time.

cards.back: Ionic or covalent? Metal + nonmetal (or a polyatomic ion) is ionic. Two nonmetals is covalent.
The nonmetal in an ionic name ends in -ide: chlorine → chloride, oxygen → oxide, nitrogen → nitride.
Never. Na₂O is sodium oxide, not disodium oxide.
Keeps its own name, with no -ide: NaNO₃ is sodium nitrate.
The metal's charge. Only for metals with more than one charge (Fe, Cu, Pb, Sn). Never for Groups 1, 2 and 13.
mono 1, di 2, tri 3, tetra 4, penta 5, hexa 6. The second element always gets one; the first never gets mono.

checks.prompt: What is the correct name of K₂S?
checks.explanation: K₂S is ionic (metal + nonmetal), so no prefixes, and potassium is in Group 1, so no numeral. Sulfur becomes sulfide. Adding di- for the 2 potassiums is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Which compound's name needs a Roman numeral?
checks.explanation: Lead can have more than one charge, so its name needs a numeral: PbCl₂ is lead(II) chloride. Mg (Group 2) and Al (Group 13) have only one charge, so they never get one. Putting a numeral on every metal is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: What is the correct name of SO₂?
checks.explanation: S and O are both nonmetals, so use prefixes: no mono on sulfur, and di- for 2 oxygens. Roman numerals are only for ionic compounds with metals like Fe or Cu, so sulfur(II) oxide is the common mistake.

steps.text: Ionic or covalent? Nickel is a metal and phosphate is a polyatomic ion, so it is ionic: no prefixes. Nickel is a transition metal, so its name needs a Roman numeral.
Find the total negative charge. There are 2 phosphates, each −3: 2 × (−3) = −6.
The nickels must cancel it, so the 3 nickels total +6. Divide by the number of nickel atoms: +6 ÷ 3 = +2 each.
Check: 3(+2) + 2(−3) = +6 − 6 = 0. Phosphate keeps its name. Answer: **nickel(II) phosphate**, not nickel(III). The 3 tells how many nickels, not the charge.

checks.prompt: Your turn: sulfate is SO₄²⁻. What is the total negative charge in Cr₂(SO₄)₃?
checks.explanation: There are 3 sulfates, each −2: 3 × (−2) = −6. Counting only one sulfate (−2) is the common mistake. +6 is the total positive charge the 2 chromiums must have.

checks.prompt: Your turn: oxide is O²⁻. What is the correct name of Mn₂O₃?
checks.explanation: Three O²⁻ give −6. Two manganese atoms share +6, so each is +3: manganese(III) oxide. Copying the subscript 2 as the numeral is the common mistake, and ionic names never use prefixes.

sections.title: Naming ionic compounds with transition metals

checks.prompt: In the name iron(III) chloride, what does the Roman numeral III tell you?

options.text: Each iron ion has a +3 charge

checks.explanation: Like saying which size coffee you want, the Roman numeral is the size of the charge, not a count of atoms. Iron(III) means Fe³⁺. Iron(III) chloride is FeCl₃, with only 1 iron.

checks.prompt: Oxide is O²⁻. What is the correct name of Fe₂O₃?
checks.explanation: Total negative: 3 × (−2) = −6. Two irons must total +6, so each is +6 ÷ 2 = +3. Check: 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0. Iron has more than one charge, so it needs the numeral: iron(III) oxide. Using the subscript 2 as the numeral is the common mistake, and ionic names never use prefixes.

sections.title: Naming covalent molecular compounds

checks.prompt: Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals. What is the correct name of CO?
checks.explanation: Covalent, so use prefixes. The first element gets a prefix except mono, so just carbon. The second element always gets a prefix and -ide: monoxide. Answer: carbon monoxide.

checks.prompt: Sulfur and oxygen are both nonmetals. Complete the name of SO₃: sulfur ___
checks.explanation: Covalent, so use prefixes. One sulfur gets no prefix (no mono on the first element). Three oxygens → tri + oxide = trioxide. Answer: sulfur trioxide.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain why CaCl₂ is named calcium chloride but SCl₂ is named sulfur dichloride.
